cover.notes:
Hi, I'm Dylan Couzon. I'm a researcher in Developer Relations at Qdrant. If someone offered you a cheaper embedding model on Monday, how much would it cost you to try it? The answer might include re-embedding the corpus and building another index. I wanted to see what happens if I keep the index I've already paid for and swap the code that turns the query into a vector.

[Trace the three paths into the cluster.] Each path here is a different way of encoding the same query. Every path searches the same documents. One of them can do it with a lookup table. I'll show you how I built it, then we'll race it against the model that built the index.

every-query.notes:
Take the query on the screen, "hiking boots for wide feet." Follow it until it turns into a vector. Only then can I ask the index for nearby documents. With Stella, a 400-million-parameter English embedding model, the first step took 31.6 milliseconds on my laptop CPU. The clock on the slide stops before I look up a single boot.

With a cache hit I can reuse the work. A new query pays for it in full. And I'm using the same large model that encoded the documents, even though I can spread the cost of encoding those documents over all the searches they serve.

forever.notes:
[Let the query line draw.] Follow the line that flattens out. I pay for each document when I index it. Then I get to reuse its vector, the HNSW graph, and the quantized codes on every search. Those assets can last for years. The other line keeps rising because fresh queries keep coming in. An agent can make several searches to finish one task, so I can pay that query cost several times before the user gets an answer.

The same asymmetry makes a model migration awkward. If I change the document encoder, I have to go back to the corpus, re-embed it, and rebuild the index. If I need to keep search online, I can end up running both indexes and both ingestion pipelines while I check the new ranking. That's a lot of work to get a cheaper query. What if I could change the query encoder and keep using the index I already serve?

zero-def.notes:
By "zero compute" I mean zero neural inference at query time. I still tokenize the text, look up rows, and average them. That work takes microseconds on my laptop. The search starts as soon as I have a vector, and the graph still has to find neighbors for it.

I can do the expensive work ahead of time because I know which document vectors I'm going to search. That gives me a target for the table. It also gives me a target for a small transformer, if I want to spend a little more on the query.

dial.notes:
I call the family Constella. Start with the documents in the middle. Stella encoded them once. Now follow the paths from the query side. I can call Stella, call Nano, a 34.5-million-parameter transformer, or call Zero, the table. The request changes which query vector I produce. All three use the same document vectors, graph, and index. I can try a different encoder on the very next request without re-indexing anything.

Imagine I'm building search for a shop. I could use Zero while someone types, give Nano a turn when they pause, and spend the full Stella budget when they hit Enter. That's one policy I'd test. The application already knows which of those events just happened. I can choose the encoder there and send along the search settings that suit it. On a device, that choice also changes what I have to ship.

device.notes:
The area of each box is the size of the encoder files I would ship. I can encode the documents with the big model in the cloud and run the query encoder where the user is. Stella means shipping nearly 1,670 MiB of files. The two smaller boxes are 132 MiB for Nano and 90 MiB for Zero. Zero's int8 table alone accounts for about 31 megabytes of that. These are file sizes. I'd measure resident memory separately.

The times come from the CPU on my M5 Pro with four threads, one query at a time. Nano takes a little over two milliseconds. Zero takes 44 microseconds. Compare that with the roughly 32 milliseconds I started with. I can only use those smaller files with my existing index if their query vectors work with Stella's document vectors.

copy.notes:
Start with the single query that forks here. I send the same text through Stella and through the student. Stella gives me the target vector. I save that target and use the difference between the two outputs to train the student. I can do the initial vector fit from those outputs alone, without asking anyone to judge which documents belong at the top.

The index at the end of the diagram is already built. It gives the student a fixed space to work in. Matching the number of dimensions is the easy bit. During the fit I want to match what Stella puts in those dimensions for the same text. Then I can put the student's vector into the same search path and measure what it retrieves. The simplest student I tried stores one vector per token.

zero-mech.notes:
[Follow the highlighted rows from the tokens to the output.] For "cheap flights Paris to Rome," I use Stella's WordPiece tokenizer. Each token ID points at one of 30,522 rows. Each row has 1,024 numbers, so I can combine them directly into a vector with the same dimensions as the documents. If a token repeats, its row gets a weight proportional to the square root of its count. That gives repeats more weight with diminishing returns. I take the weighted mean and normalize it. If you come from Lucene, think of a term-weight lookup that happens to emit a dense query vector.

To build the released table, I started the rows from Stella's own token vectors. I trained the pooled output to match Stella's query vectors and used Stella's scores as another target on paired examples. Then I trained the table to rank relevant documents ahead of negatives from the frozen document vectors. I ran that training on a desktop RTX 3080. When I serve the table, I fetch its int8 rows and pool them. The expensive model has already done its part.

Look at which information goes into that average. Each token ID contributes a row and a count. What happens if I keep the words and change the route?

order.notes:
Suppose I want to go from Paris to Rome. If I reverse those cities, I'd like a different ticket. Zero gets the same bag of tokens either way. I look up the same rows with the same weights. Both queries produce exactly the same vector.

I wanted to see how much a contextual encoder would gain here. I wrote 24 pairs of queries where reversing the direction changes the answer. I gave each pair two passages, one intended for each direction. I counted a pair as a success only if the right passage came first on both queries. Stella changed its vector on every reversal. [click] Stella ranked the right passage first in both directions on 4 of 24 pairs. All four successes were unit conversions.

That's a small exploratory test. The query and passage pairs are in the repository. For Zero, this kind of reversal disappears during pooling. For Stella, a change in the query vector was easy to measure. Getting both rankings right was harder. Nano gives me a way to keep a contextual encoder on the query side at a smaller cost.

nano.notes:
I started Nano with a pretrained bge-small backbone. The projection in the middle takes its features into Stella's 1,024-dimensional space. I trained the backbone and projection together against Stella's vectors for millions of query texts and for document passages. The targets for that fit were the teacher's embeddings, so Nano's optimization needed no relevance labels. Stella still encodes the corpus that Nano searches.

The two hardware blocks tell you which work went where. I did Zero's full training and the search for Nano's training recipe on a desktop RTX 3080 with 10 GB of memory. Nano's final optimization ran once on an A100. It took 57.3 hours, which came to about $95 at the recorded rate. That's the bill for the final optimization. Data prep, recipe search, and failed runs add to the cost of building the encoder.

I now have two cheaper ways to produce a vector for the same documents. I need to find out what each one gives up in the ranking.

survive.notes:
For this chart, I score every candidate against the documents exactly. That way I can see what each encoder does to the ranking before I introduce graph search. The bars are the mean nDCG@10 across 15 BEIR datasets, with each dataset getting the same weight. This was a registered descriptive evaluation.

Use Stella as the reference. Nano keeps 90.5% of its score, and Zero keeps 81.4%. Both score higher than the BM25 baseline on this average. If you run search for one of those workloads, the average is a poor substitute for your own row. Quora is a duplicate-question task, where a query can look a lot like the question it should find. Zero keeps 95% of Stella's score there. On TREC-COVID and FiQA it keeps about two thirds. The cheaper encoder can cross your relevance floor on one workload and fall short on another.

I'd use the exact numbers to decide which encoders deserve a place in the latency test. Once I put the graph back into the request, a second question comes up. How much of that encoding time do I get to keep?

bet.notes:
Take the two small encoders on this laptop. Zero is [N] times faster than Nano at producing the vector. That's where I'd stop the clock if I were benchmarking the encoder. [click] Now keep it running until the results come back. What would you bet on for the speedup? Shout a number or put one in the Zoom chat.

[Take guesses. Keep a guess to compare with the replay.] Keep that number in mind when we watch where each lane spends its time.

race.notes:
[Switch the shared screen to the demo. Open Race and press Space. Play the recorded fallback if the replay is unavailable.]

I measured these queries one encoder at a time on this laptop. The lanes replay those per-query timings, so they can line up on screen without competing for the same CPU. The replay covers [3,452] questions. The dense lanes use one Stella index with [2.7M] Wikipedia passages. Qdrant Edge is running inside the demo process.

Follow the join in each bar. Teal is the time up to the point where I have a query vector. Orange is the time from there through the graph search. Start with Stella to see how much the encoder matters when it's the large transformer. Then watch Zero. The join comes early enough that you spend most of the race watching it search.

[Let the replay run. Point out the encoding and search segments for Nano and Zero on the same query. Compare the full timings shown for the two lanes.]

Which guess is closest to the full search result? [Read back the displayed Nano and Zero totals and the speedup for the full request.] The encoding gain is still there. Graph search takes up more of the time that remains. This is an exploratory replay on one laptop. If I were setting a latency budget for my own service, I'd time both parts there and check the full request against the relevance I need.

[Return to the recovery slide.]

recovery.notes:
All three dense encoders walk the same HNSW graph. Its links connect document vectors. To measure how well an encoder searches it, I first run an exact search with that encoder's vector and save its top 10. Then I count how many of those documents come back through the graph at each setting of hnsw_ef. Stella has its own reference list. So do Nano and Zero.

[If the recovery chart is available, use this paragraph and trace a fixed hnsw_ef across the curves.] This is the Wikipedia index from the race, with binary quantization and rescoring. Where Zero's curve sits lower at the same hnsw_ef, it finds a smaller share of its own exact neighbors than Stella finds of its own.

In the paper's graph tests, fitted tables often needed a wider search to match the teacher's recovery rate. Each encoder had its own exact neighbors as the reference. A wider search takes time and can get a ranking closer to what that encoder returns with an exact scan. I'd still use judged relevance to decide whether those are the documents I want. We can watch the exact-neighbor count change on a query from the room.

live.notes:
[Switch to the demo and open Live. Take a query from the room or Zoom chat. Enter it and run all four columns.]

You can give me something you'd look up in Wikipedia. Stella, Nano, and Zero all search the same document vectors. BM25 gives us a lexical reference over the same passages. Watch the split between encoding and search, then look at the first passage each column returns. Read the title and the first line with me. Which one would you open?

[Read the first results aloud. Ask what the audience wanted to find. Switch on the exact check and compare the dense columns.]

This count is specific to each encoder. In the Zero column I'm asking how many of Zero's exact top 10 the graph found. If Stella and Zero both recover all 10, their exact lists can still be different. Now I'll change hnsw_ef and run the same text again. We keep the encoder and index in place, so we can see what changing the search breadth buys on this query.

[Lower hnsw_ef and rerun. Raise it and rerun. Read out the search times and exact-neighbor counts that appear. If the first query barely changes, take another from the room or Zoom. Use the recorded fallback if live search is unavailable.]

Watch the search segment after I turn the setting up. Check whether the extra time brought any of the exact neighbors back. If the count stays put, compare what we spent for the same recall. I'd use a set of judged queries to decide whether the trade holds across my traffic. That same set can save me time before I even pick a teacher.

[Return to the deck.]

worst.notes:
I'd expected the strongest retriever to give me the strongest cheap student. To test that, I fitted one lookup table for each of 10 public embedding models in the registered comparison. Each model kept its own document index. The equation shows the ridge fit for those screening tables. X is the token counts divided by the number of tokens in the query, and Y is the model's own query vectors. I fit the rows so the pooled vectors approach Y. The penalty keeps the rows close to what the teacher outputs when I encode each token alone.

Each screen took four to seven minutes on an A100. Then I measured exact ranking on six BEIR datasets. [Point to gte-large, then Stella.] The farther a dot is to the right, the better the original retriever. The higher it is, the better the table. gte-large is farthest to the right and gave me the weakest table of these 10 models. Stella gave me the strongest table. Even close agreement with the teacher's query vectors could go with worse ranking. Once a fit takes minutes, I can spend my time measuring the ranking I want on the queries I serve.

recipe.notes:
I'd start Monday by sampling queries from my own traffic and getting relevance judgments. I'd choose a minimum nDCG@10 and a p95 latency budget before I pick an encoder. The benchmark averages tell me which changes are worth a look. Those two limits tell me if I can ship one.

I'd run exact search for each candidate over the document vectors I have in production. If an encoder already falls below my relevance floor there, I can see the ranking problem before I add the graph. Then I'd sweep hnsw_ef for each encoder. On a quantized index I'd sweep oversampling too, so I can see what I gain by rescoring a larger group of candidates. I'd measure nDCG@10 again at the settings I can serve.

Finally, I'd time completed requests, from text in to results out. I'd record p95 with encoding and search in the same request on the system I plan to use. Then I'd pick the cheapest encoder and search settings that clear both limits. If I serve more than one budget, I'd carry the search settings with the encoder choice. The index can serve each of them.

close.notes:
If you've already paid to build an index, it can be the same index you use to try a cheaper query encoder. Start with a batch you can judge. See where you'd set the dial for that traffic.

[Leave the paper preview and repository QR on screen when available.] Zero, Nano, and the Stella document encoder are on Hugging Face and in FastEmbed. The install command is on the slide, and the QR code links the models and the code. The paper preview has the benchmark numbers and how I measured them. Thanks for the queries, in the room and on Zoom.

b-datasets.notes: Quora was at 95% of Stella's score for Zero, while TREC-COVID and FiQA were both at 67%. Nano kept 85% to 99% across the other datasets. FEVER is the exception to that Nano range, and its training data was in Zero's pool while Nano left it out.

b-msmarco.notes: On the binary-quantized million-passage MS MARCO index, the sum of separate encoding and search medians put Zero at about 19 times Stella's speed and 2.2 times Nano's, at lower nDCG@10. For this exploratory comparison, I used each encoder's fastest setting within 1% of its own exact score. In the whole-request comparison on those passages, BM25 took 0.66 ms at 0.4895 nDCG@10 and Zero took 1.11 ms at 0.6094, so BM25 saved 0.45 ms and Zero scored 24.5% higher.

b-edge.notes: I put all 30,522 rows in a Qdrant Edge shard and fetched them by token ID before pooling and searching. Across 500 queries the vectors exactly matched the released encoder, with a maximum difference of zero. On this laptop the lookup path added about 0.25 ms compared with the in-memory NumPy table.

b-routing.notes: The oracle used relevance judgments to pick Zero or Nano and scored 0.547 against 0.516 for always running Nano. At the same Nano share, query length, subwords per word, and pooled vector norm beat random routing by at most 0.005 nDCG@10. I'd start with a policy based on what the user is doing, such as typing, pausing, or submitting a search.
